desc:
You must split the elements of nums into groups so that every element belongs to exactly one group and, inside each group, the elements taken in their original order are strictly increasing. The elements of a group do not have to be adjacent in nums.

Return the smallest possible number of groups. For nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6] the answer is 3 (for example the groups 3, 4, 5, 9, 1, 2, 6 and 1), while for a strictly decreasing array of length n the answer is n.
hints: Think of building the groups one element at a time. Each new element either extends an existing group or starts a new one. Which group should it extend?

An element x can extend a group whose last element is smaller than x. Extending the group with the largest such last element wastes the least: the groups with small ends stay available for small values.

Keep the sorted list of group ends. For x, replace the largest end that is smaller than x with x, or insert x as a brand new end if no end is smaller. The size of the list is the answer (it equals the length of the longest non-increasing subsequence).
editorial: Process the array left to right and maintain the last element of every group in a sorted list ends. A new element x can join any group whose end is strictly smaller than x. Among those, joining the one with the largest end is never worse: it uses up the least flexible end and leaves the groups with smaller ends free for smaller future values (an exchange argument). If no end is smaller than x, a new group must start.

With binary search, i = bisect_left(ends, x) is the number of ends smaller than x. If i == 0 insert x at the front as a new group; otherwise overwrite ends[i-1] with x. The list stays sorted, and its final length is the answer. The cost is O(n log n) to search plus the list insertion at the front, fine for n = 5,000.

There is a neat characterisation of the same number: it equals the length of the longest non-increasing subsequence. Such a subsequence can never fit into one increasing group (two of its elements would be in decreasing or equal order), so you need at least that many groups, and the greedy above shows that this many always suffice (this is Dilworth's theorem for this order).
